text: Two hundred thousand tonnes of rock. That is roughly how much was cut away, by hand, with hammers and chisels, to leave behind a single temple. Nothing here was built. Not one block was carried in. Workers started at the top of a basalt hill and carved downwards, removing everything that was not the temple. This is Kailasa, at Ellora in Maharashtra, and it is more than twelve hundred years old. In the next few minutes you'll see how big it really is, how long it may have taken, who ordered it, and how to see it for yourself.
Kailasa. The temple carved from one rock.

Ellora sits on the Deccan plateau in Maharashtra, about thirty kilometres northwest of Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, the city once called Aurangabad. The famous painted caves of Ajanta are about a hundred kilometres away, which is why most people see the two together. But Ellora is not one monument. It is a whole cliff of them.

Thirty-four caves are open to visitors, cut into a basalt cliff that stretches for more than two kilometres. Twelve are Buddhist, seventeen are Hindu, and five are Jain, carved between about six hundred and one thousand CE. Three faiths, side by side, in one rock face. UNESCO made Ellora a World Heritage Site in nineteen eighty-three. And right in the middle, numbered Cave Sixteen, is the one that stops everyone in their tracks.

The rock itself matters. Ellora is carved into basalt in the Charanandri hills, part of the Deccan Traps, layer upon layer of ancient lava flows that cover much of western India. Basalt is hard and heavy. It does not forgive mistakes. There is no way to glue back a broken nose or a chipped elephant. Every cut had to be right the first time.

Here is how it was done. Most earlier rock-cut temples were dug inwards from the front, like a cave. Kailasa was carved from the top down. First, three huge trenches were cut vertically into the hillside, isolating a giant block of rock. Then the carvers worked down through that block, shaping towers, halls, pillars and statues as they went. What looks like a building standing in a courtyard is really what was left behind when everything else was taken away.

So how big is it? The courtyard measures about eighty-two metres by forty-six metres at its base. To put that in perspective, here is the Parthenon in Athens, one of the most famous temples on Earth. Its base is about sixty-nine and a half metres by thirty-one. Kailasa's courtyard covers almost twice that area, and every square metre of it was cut out of solid rock.

Now look up. The top of the tower over the sanctuary stands about thirty-two and a half metres above the courtyard floor. That is roughly the height of a ten storey building, and more than three times as tall as the Parthenon's columns, which are about ten metres. Remember, the carvers did not climb up to make that tower. They started at its tip and worked downwards.

And the rock they removed? Estimates put it at about eighty-five thousand cubic metres, weighing roughly two hundred thousand tonnes. An Olympic swimming pool holds about two thousand five hundred cubic metres of water. So the stone hauled out of this one pit would fill around thirty-four Olympic pools. All of it broken, carried and dumped by human hands.

How long did that take? Nobody recorded it. The archaeologist M. K. Dhavalikar made an estimate. He assumed one person could cut around four cubic feet of rock a day, and worked out that two hundred and fifty labourers could have finished the main temple in about five and a half years. That is a calculation, not a record, and it does not include the finest sculpture. Dhavalikar thought some of the most famous panels were carved three or four decades after the main shrine was done.

So who ordered it? Most historians credit Krishna the First of the Rashtrakuta dynasty, who ruled from about seven fifty-six to seven seventy-three CE. His predecessor Dantidurga left an inscription in the cave right next door, Cave Fifteen, and he may have started the work. Either way, Kailasa was being carved in the middle of the eighth century, when the Rashtrakutas were becoming one of the most powerful dynasties in India.

We even have a reaction from the time. A copper plate inscription found in Vadodara, dated to around eight twelve CE, says the king built a temple so wondrous that even the gods and the architect were astonished. Later, a Marathi legend added a story. A queen vowed not to eat until she saw the temple's top, and an architect named Kokasa promised to deliver it by carving from the top down. It's a legend, but it shows people were trying to explain this place for centuries.

Walk through the gateway and the details pile up. Carved elephants run around the base, as if they are holding the whole temple up. A stone bridge links the Nandi hall to the main shrine. Two tall pillars stand in the courtyard. The main hall rests on sixteen pillars. A columned gallery three storeys high wraps around the edges, and five separate shrines sit around the courtyard, three of them for the river goddesses Ganga, Yamuna and Saraswati.

The most famous panel shows Ravana trying to lift Mount Kailasa, the mountain home of Shiva, while Shiva calmly holds it down. Some scholars think the temple may even have taken its name from this scene. Look closely at the ceilings too. Only traces remain of the paintings that once covered the temple, and some of the colour you see is far later, added in the eighteenth century under Ahilyabai Holkar.

If you want to see it, Ellora is open from nine in the morning to five in the evening, and it's closed on Tuesdays. Ajanta, by the way, is closed on Mondays, so plan the two around each other. The nearest airport and railway station are in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, about thirty kilometres away. October to March is the most comfortable time to go, which means right now. One honest tip: arrive at opening time. By late morning Cave Sixteen fills up, and the afternoon sun bakes the courtyard.

So here is Kailasa at true scale. A courtyard almost twice the area of the Parthenon. A tower about thirty-two metres tall, carved from the top down. Around two hundred thousand tonnes of basalt removed, with no machines, more than twelve hundred years ago.

Now I want your take. Do you think a team of a few hundred people really carved this in under six years, or did it take generations? Tell me in the comments. And subscribe to True Scale for more of India's wonders, drawn to true scale.
